note: Start with sharp carbon-number splits to recover the valuable C5 blend and a C4-light overhead, using moderate column severity.
notebook:
PLAN: Build an efficient blend-oriented sequence: (1) C4/C5 feed split, (2) recover C5 blend overhead, (3) recover C4/C3 products and C6-paraffin blend, then tune costly columns and test selective pure-product upgrades. Step 1 now: establish root and C5 splitter performance/cost.
The C5 and C6-paraffin blends contain most feed value, while C3/C4 cuts are also easy. Avoid difficult isomer separation initially. Moderate stages/reflux should suffice for adjacent carbon-number cuts; pressure drop may reduce utility cost.

note: Sharpen the root and C5/C6 split enough to obtain the first sellable blend and establish a realistic cost/revenue baseline.
notebook:
PLAN: Build an efficient blend-oriented sequence: (1) sharp C5/C6 feed split, (2) recover C5 blend overhead, (3) recover C4/C3 products and C6-paraffin blend, then tune costly columns and test selective pure-product upgrades. Step 1 now: sharpen root and C5 splitter.
Initial 45-stage root and B columns were far too sloppy: root T only 38% n-butane and BT only 28% n-pentane. R4 confirms 60/2.5 is still sloppy and expensive. Raise severity substantially; C5 blend alone is worth roughly $550M/yr before discount, so recovery can justify cost. Avoid difficult isomer separations initially.

note: Move the root cut below all C5 by lowering boil-up, and sharpen the C5/C6 split with higher reflux to obtain the first valuable blend.
notebook:
PLAN: Build an efficient blend-oriented sequence: (1) sharp C4/C5 feed split, (2) recover C5 blend overhead, (3) recover C4/C3 products and C6-paraffin blend, then tune costly columns and test selective pure-product upgrades. Step 1 now: sharpen root and C5 splitter.
Initial splits were far too sloppy. Root 80/4/4 cuts within C5: T contains 353 mol/s C5, leaving too little for B. Need lower root boil-up to move C5 downward while retaining high reflux. B also needs higher reflux/lower distillate to exclude C6. C5 blend is about $619M/yr at blend pricing, enough to justify two efficient columns. Avoid difficult isomer separations initially.

note: Reduce capital and internal traffic at the root while moving C5 into the bottoms; use a smaller, sharper C5/C6 splitter to target the first sellable C5 blend.
notebook:
PLAN: Build an efficient blend-oriented sequence: (1) sharp C4/C5 feed split, (2) recover C5 blend overhead, (3) recover C4/C3 products and C6-paraffin blend, then tune costly columns and test selective pure-product upgrades. Step 1 now: obtain a converged, economical C5-blend baseline.
High boil-up at the root sends essentially all C5 overhead; low boil-up is required to retain it in B. R100 confirms that 90-100 stages and 8-10 ratios are excessively costly (~$844M for two columns), while still not yielding a blend. Try fewer stages and very low root boil-up, with high B boil-up to lift C5 overhead. C5 blend revenue potential is ~$670M/yr; the two columns must be kept well below this. Avoid isomer separations initially.

note: Interpolate the root boil-up between the C4-contaminated and C5-contaminated runs, and reduce the second column's size while preserving its C5/C6 split.
notebook:
PLAN: Build an efficient blend-oriented sequence: (1) sharp C4/C5 feed split, (2) recover C5 blend overhead, (3) recover C4/C3 products and C6-paraffin blend, then tune costly columns and test selective pure-product upgrades. Step 1: establish a converged C5-blend baseline.
R145 root at boil-up 2 removes only 658 mol/s overhead, leaving ~206 mol/s C4 in B; that C4 then contaminates its nominal C5 overhead (26% N-butane). My boil-up 1 failed and 5 sent C5 overhead. Interpolate to root boil-up 3 to put the cut between C4/C5. Keep B boil-up 2.5 but reduce B to 60 stages for cost. Once C5 blend is pure, trim stages/ratios and add only high-value branches. Avoid isomer separations initially.

note: Copy the proven blend core and cut the root column’s capital and reflux cost while retaining its converged boil-up and pressure.
notebook:
PLAN: Build a profitable blend core first: (1) bank and cheapen the proven C4/C5 sequence, (2) recover additional heavy products only where net-positive, (3) tune stages and reflux, then test selected pure-product upgrades. Step 1: copy R192 and reduce its dominant root cost.
R192 earns $467M/yr from C4 and C5 blends at $364M/yr cost (reward 0.237). Its root alone costs $261M/yr, so reducing root stages 70->50 and reflux 4->3 is the clearest immediate improvement. Keep boil-up 4.0 and dp 0.2 to preserve its converged split; keep both downstream columns unchanged this run. My previous low-boil-up root attempts repeatedly failed, so use the proven R192 operating region rather than interpolating further. Root discards about 299 mol/s N-pentane in B; heavy-branch recovery is a later opportunity, but only after establishing a cheaper valid core.

note: Keep the cheaper, C5-rich root split and increase C4/C5 splitter reflux to reject the extra C5 from the C4 overhead.
notebook:
PLAN: Build a profitable blend core first: (1) bank and cheapen the proven C4/C5 sequence, (2) recover additional heavy products only where net-positive, (3) tune stages and reflux, then test selected pure-product upgrades. Step 1: retain the cheaper root and repair C4 purity at the C4/C5 splitter.
The cheaper 50/3/4 root produces 51 mol/s more saleable C5 than R192 (TBB revenue $393M versus $351M), but its heavier TB feed makes TBT only 77% C4. All C4 already reports to TBT; the problem is 85 mol/s C5 leakage overhead. Increasing TB reflux 4->6 should reduce overhead takeoff and retain C5 in TBB, potentially restoring the $117M C4 sale while keeping the extra C5. This is preferable to simply restoring the expensive root. R192 remains the fallback: 70/4/4 root, 50/2.5/2.5 T, 60/4/4 TB gives reward 0.237.

note: Use the best proven blend core and test recovery of the very valuable C6 paraffin blend from the heavy bottoms.
notebook:
PLAN: Build a profitable blend core first: (1) bank and cheapen the proven C4/C5 sequence, (2) recover additional heavy products only where net-positive, (3) tune stages and reflux, then test selected pure-product upgrades. Step 2: copy the best 60/4/4 blend core and add a C6-paraffin/heavy splitter on B.
My 50/3/4 root recovers extra C5 but contaminates TBT; even TB reflux 6 leaves C4 at only 92%. R285 is the better base: reward 0.238, C4 revenue $116.7M and C5 $350.6M. Its 2040 mol/s B contains about 970 mol/s C6 paraffins, worth roughly $1.15B/yr as their 85% blend. An 80-stage, reflux-4 splitter should approach the difficult N-hexane/methylcyclopentane cut; its cost should be well below the available revenue if 95% blend purity is reached. Next, if BT qualifies, add an easy naphthene/C7+ split on BB.

note: Revert to the profitable core, reject residual C5 overhead from the heavy branch, and then apply the promising C6-paraffin split to the C5-free bottoms.
notebook:
PLAN: Build a profitable blend core first: (1) bank and cheapen the proven C4/C5 sequence, (2) recover additional heavy products only where net-positive, (3) tune stages and reflux, then test selected pure-product upgrades. Step 2: remove residual C5 from root bottoms, then recover the C6-paraffin blend.
The direct B split failed because its 866 mol/s tops contained about 30% C5; however, after C5 removal its C6 paraffins would be roughly 97% of the remainder. R334's alternative two-column ordering was wrong: its first split sent still more C5 and C6 overhead together. Revert to R285 and use B at 60/4/1 as a C5-overhead polishing column, then BB at the already tested 80/4/3 C6/heavy split. This should sell both residual C5 and the very valuable C6 blend. Avoid root dp=0.1, which R335 showed destroys the core split.

note: Restore the best proven core and raise root boil-up to recover more of the valuable C5 currently lost to the unsold heavy bottoms.
notebook:
PLAN: Build a profitable blend core first: (1) bank and cheapen the proven C4/C5 sequence, (2) recover additional heavy products only where net-positive, (3) tune stages and reflux. Step 1: increase C5 recovery into the proven downstream splitter.
R285 is the best visible core (0.238): 60/4/4 root, 50/2.5/2.5 T, 60/4/4 TB. It sells 342 mol/s C4 and 394 C5 for $467M, but 267 mol/s C5 remains in unsold root bottoms. Each extra mol/s C5 recovered is worth about $0.89M/yr, so raising root boil-up may pay even with extra duty. C6 carried upward should be rejected by T into TB bottoms and must be watched. Heavy-branch tests were strongly net-negative: B polishing plus 80-100 stage C6 splitting cost $184-241M and still sold no C6. Trimming TB to 50/3/3 destroyed both blends; do not repeat. Root 50/3/4 also degraded the core. Avoid root dp=0.1.

notebook:

Avoid double effect (no heat link), root dp .1, and TB 50/3/3.

A conventional TT split should recover ~$70M C4 and a small TTT ethane splitter should unlock ~$61M C3. Ethane itself is worth only ~$4M, so its purity is secondary.

notebook:

R625 earns 0.422 with a 25% liquid side draw at TT stage 20: TTS is 97% C3, TTB is 95% C4, while TBT/TBB retain the core C4/C5 blends. Its root costs $260M/yr, 68% of total cost; reducing root stages 50 to 40 saved almost nothing, so reflux/boil-up and pressure are the important levers. Conventional light splitters failed because C4 and C3 purity were inadequate. Heavy C6 recovery was strongly negative. Preserve R625 as fallback and change only root energetics.

R671 adds a 40-stage, 3/3 column at TTT: its 104 mol/s bottoms is a saleable C3 blend, adding $26.7M/yr for only $9.5M/yr. Its four-column core is R625, which earns 0.422; reducing side draw below 25% destroys TTB C4 purity, and root reflux 3.0 badly shifts the cut and loses C5 recovery. Root dominates cost ($260M/yr), but stage reduction saved little. Heavy C6 recovery was strongly negative. Preserve R671 as fallback and focus next on modest downstream energy reductions or improving TTT recovery.

Heavy C6 recovery has been strongly negative. Preserve the C4/C5 blend core and TT side draw at 25%.
